summary.text: When Pluto carried off Persephone with Zeus' connivance, Demeter wandered the earth with torches until she came to Eleusis in mortal guise — and when the Maid ate a pomegranate seed in the underworld, the goddess' grief withered the crops until a compromise split the year between mother and king of the dead.

chapters.title: The Maid taken
chapters.text: Apollodorus says Pluto seized Persephone secretly, with Zeus' help. Demeter learned from the Hermionians that the god of the dead had taken her, and in anger she quit Olympus. Ovid places the rape in Sicily: while Proserpina gathered flowers by Lake Pergus near Henna, Dis saw her, loved her, and plunged with his chariot through the pool of Cyane — and the nymph Arethusa, whose stream runs beneath the earth, later told Ceres where her daughter had gone. Pausanias records rival Greek localizations at Eleusis and Argos.

chapters.title: Torches and Eleusis
chapters.text: Demeter roamed the whole earth by night and day with torches in search of the Maid. Coming in the likeness of a mortal woman to Eleusis, she was welcomed by Celeus and Metaneira; she nursed their infant Demophon in the fire to make him immortal, but Metaneira's cry broke the charm. For Triptolemus, eldest son of Metaneira, she fashioned a chariot of winged dragons and gave him wheat to sow over the inhabited world.

chapters.title: The pomegranate seed
chapters.text: When Zeus ordered Pluto to send the Maid up, Pluto gave her a seed of a pomegranate to eat so that she might not stay long with her mother. Not foreseeing the consequence, she swallowed it — and because Ascalaphus bore witness that she had eaten, Demeter laid a heavy rock on him in Hades. For that one seed she must spend a third of every year below with Pluto and the rest with the gods; Ovid and Hyginus also reckon half the revolving year with each parent.

chapters.title: The turning seasons
chapters.text: While Persephone dwells in the house of Hades, Demeter's sorrow withholds growth from the earth; when the Maid returns to Olympus, the world blooms again. The compromise is the mythic root of sowing and harvest — agriculture bound to the rhythm of descent and return.
